questions.stem: An 18-year-old man presented with fatigue, malaise, and sore throat, nausea, and anorexia. He could not recall any sick contacts. On examination, there was an exudative pharyngitis and tender splenomegaly. Investigations: Group A streptococcus rapid antigen negative CMV IgM positive Heterophile antibody positive EBV testing: VCA IgM positive VCA IgG positive EA IgG positive EBNA IgG negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: EBV The serologic results and heterophile antibody test support the diagnosis of EBV infection. IgM and IgG antibodies to the viral capsid antigen (VCA) are usually positive at the onset of symptoms, as are IgG antibodies to the early antigen (EA). EBNA antibodies, however, appear weeks later and then persist. They should be negative in the early stages of clinical illness, as they are here. Exudative pharyngitis in EBV can be confused for S. pyogenes, though rapid testing is negative. Of note a back-up culture or NAAT test should be performed to confirm the rapid test. CMV IgM is most likely a cross-reaction as IgM can cross-react with EBV VCA.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q3

questions.stem: A 19-year-old male presented to the student health clinic with several days of fever, sore throat, and profound fatigue. He has evident tonsillitis on exam and has some palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The provider suspected possible streptococcal pharyngitis and prescribed amoxicillin. The next day he developed a pruritic, maculopapular rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his illness?
questions.explanation: Epstein–Barr virus This patient most likely has infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV . He has tonsillitis with prominent adenopathy and fatigue. Splenomegaly may also be identified on exam, and laboratory evaluation can show atypical lymphocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and hepatitis. Patients with active EBV infection may develop drug eruptions when prescribed penicillins.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q29

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was brought in by ambulance after being found unconscious. His partner gave a collateral history of preceding symptoms for 3 weeks of fevers, headaches, and new-onset seizures. He was known to have HIV but had not been on antiretroviral therapy or taking antibiotic prophylaxis. The patient was originally from Brazil but immigrated to the United States 2 years ago. On physical exam, the patient was somnolent with rightsided upper and lower extremity weakness. Investigations: CD4 count 23 cells/μL HIV viral load 76,850 copies/mL Serum Toxoplasma IgG serologies negative CSF EBV PCR negative CSF VDRL negative MRI brain: 3 discrete hypodense masses in the cerebral cortex with contrast ring enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chagas brain abscess In patients from endemic regions, Trypanosoma cruzi can cause acute or reactivation disease, particularly in patients with advanced AIDS. The most common presentation is CNS reactivation leading to meningoencephalitis or brain abscesses, which presents very similarly to Toxoplasma with ring-enhancing lesions on MRI imaging. The negative serum Toxoplasma serologies and EBV PCR in the CSF make other causes such as toxoplasmic encephalitis or primary CNS lymphoma less likely while the patient’s country of origin in South America is endemic for Chagas disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q24

questions.question: Interpret the timing and duration of VCA IgM, VCA IgG, and EBNA in EBV infectious mononucleosis (are they present at presentation of infectious mononucleosis and how long do they persist?).
questions.question_raw: Q90 2023 Day 1. EBV interpretation of serologies (are they present at presentation of infectious mono and how long are they present for): VCA IgM, VCA IgG, Viral nucleocapsid (EBNA). (MICRO)

parts.text: Interpret timing/duration of VCA IgM, VCA IgG, and EBNA in EBV infectious mononucleosis.

parts_raw.text: Interpret timing/duration of VCA IgM, VCA IgG, and EBNA in EBV infectious mononucleosis

questions.model_answer: VCA IgM: present at clinical presentation (100%), transient - persists ~4-8 weeks then falls (virtually diagnostic of acute infection, not seen in the general population). VCA IgG: present at clinical presentation (100%), near peak at first visit, persists lifelong (better as an epidemiologic marker of past infection than a diagnostic test). EBNA: absent at presentation - appears late, ~3-4 weeks after onset (100%), then persists lifelong; seroconversion from EBNA-negative to EBNA-positive with pre-existing VCA IgG indicates recent infection and is useful in heterophile-negative cases.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort gives peak days and an EBNA rise "around 2 months"; Mandell states EBNA appears ~3-4 weeks after onset - the durations (VCA IgM weeks, VCA IgG and EBNA lifelong) agree.

cohort_answer.text: VCA IgM: peaks at day 10, resolved by 1 month. VCA IgG: peaks at day 14, lifelong. EBNA: rises around 2 months, usually around 6 months, lasts lifelong.

questions.question: A patient is awaiting a kidney transplant. He is EBV negative. A donor kidney is available, and the donor's serology is VCA IgM negative, VCA IgG positive, EBNA positive.
questions.question_raw: A patient is awaiting a kidney transplant. He is EBV negative. A donor kidney is available, and the donor's serology is VCA IgM neg, VCA IgG pos, EBNA pos.

parts.text: Interpret the serology.
What are the clinical implications of transplanting into an EBV negative host?

parts_raw.text: Interpret the serology
What are the clinical implications of transplanting into an EBV negative host?

questions.model_answer: a) The donor is a healthy EBV-immune carrier with past (remote) infection, not acute: IgM VCA is negative (IgM VCA appears at presentation and persists only 4-8 weeks in acute infection), while IgG VCA is positive (appears at presentation, lifelong) and EBNA is positive (appears 3-4 weeks after onset, lifelong). Presence of EBNA with absent IgM VCA excludes recent/acute infection and confirms established latency. b) This is an EBV donor-positive/recipient-negative (D+/R-) mismatch. The seronegative recipient is at high risk of primary EBV infection transmitted with the graft under immunosuppression, and therefore at markedly increased risk of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD); up to half of PTLD occurs in the setting of primary EBV infection, and EBV-naive recipients (as with children) are the group at greatest risk. Implication: EBV serostatus monitoring and quantitative EBV viral-load surveillance post-transplant to allow pre-emptive reduction of immunosuppression or rituximab.

questions.question: A man with HIV who has lived in Toronto his entire life is non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy with a CD4 count of 50 cells/uL. He presents with three weeks of altered level of consciousness and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.
questions.question_raw: Gentleman with HIV has lived in Toronto his entire life. Noncompliant with ART and CD4 is 50. Presents with 3 weeks of altered LOC and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What are the four most likely organisms and the diseases they cause?

parts_raw.text: What are the 4 most likely organisms and diseases they cause?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (asymmetric, non-enhancing white-matter lesions, no mass effect; diagnosis by CSF JC virus PCR). (2) HIV-1 - HIV encephalopathy/HIV-associated dementia with diffuse symmetric white-matter signal change and atrophy. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis at CD4 <50. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningoencephalitis with basal meningitis and infarction. Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis is the other key consideration; Toxoplasma encephalitis and primary CNS lymphoma are less likely given the absence of mass effect.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort lists HSV and VZV as leading answers; in advanced HIV with subacute multifocal white-matter disease and no mass effect, PML, HIV encephalopathy, CMV and tuberculosis are the higher-yield answers.

cohort_answer.text: PML - JC Virus; CMV; HSV; VZV; TB (possible to get hydrocephalus though). Other differentials more likely to have mass effect/increased ICP: Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal. Non-infectious ddx: CNS lymphoma (causes mass effect).

parts.text: Complete the table (Nucleic Acid, Envelope, Antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Ebola, Zika.

parts_raw.text: Complete the table (Nucleic Acid, Envelope, Antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Ebola, Zika

questions.model_answer:
Mumps: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive).
Measles: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A adjunct; ribavirin unproven).
Hepatitis B: DNA; enveloped; yes - nucleos(t)ide analogues (tenofovir, entecavir), peginterferon.
EBV: DNA; enveloped; no established antiviral (aciclovir/ganciclovir have limited activity).
Ebola: RNA; enveloped; yes - monoclonal antibodies (atoltivimab-maftivimab-odesivimab [Inmazeb], ansuvimab [Ebanga]).
Zika: RNA; enveloped; none.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only measles (RNA, enveloped, ribavirin unproven, Mandell p. 2116) is covered by this chapter; the other rows are from general virology and current IDSA/CDC therapeutics.

questions.question: Regarding post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD).

parts.text: What are two risk factors for this condition?
What test can be performed on a lymph node biopsy that will support this diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 risk factors for this condition?
What test can be performed on a lymph node biopsy that will support this diagnosis?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) EBV serostatus mismatch (EBV-seropositive donor / EBV-seronegative recipient, D+/R-). (2) Intense immunosuppression, particularly T-cell-depleting induction/anti-rejection therapy (antithymocyte globulin); belatacept also increases EBV-associated PTLD. b) Detection of EBV in the tissue, most specifically EBV-encoded RNA in situ hybridization (EBER) on the lymph node biopsy.
questions.beyond_mandell: EBER in situ hybridization as the confirmatory tissue test is standard pathology practice; the chapter establishes the EBV association but does not name the specific assay.

needs: Chapter 313 — Infections in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients
questions.question: EBV-associated post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD).

parts.text: What are 2 clinical risk factors for early PTLD after solid organ transplant?
What testing method do you use to identify EBV disease on lymph node biopsy?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 clinical risk factors for early PTLD after SOT (1)
What testing method do you use to identify EBV disease on lymph node biopsy (0.5)

questions.model_answer: a) Two risk factors: (1) primary EBV infection after transplantation (EBV D+/R- mismatch, seronegative recipient) - up to half of PTLD arises with primary infection and often in EBV-naive children; (2) intensity of T-cell immunosuppression, particularly T-cell-depleting therapy such as antithymocyte globulin (also higher-risk graft type, e.g. multivisceral/intestinal). b) In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) on the biopsy tissue demonstrating nuclear staining in tumour cells.

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: Type of transplant (multivisceral high rates likely due to lymphoid tissue in transplant organs already heavily infected with EBV); Primary infection due to EBV mismatch (D+, R-); Degree of T cell immunosuppression; Time post-transplant (highest risk early in BMT where immunosuppression highest early on); Use of antithymocyte globulin; EBV-encoded small nuclear RNAs (EBERs) present in transplant organ; Late PTLD associated with chronic GVHD
